chapter: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
title: Modulating keys and the hard keys Fletcher favored
summary: Interludes and key changes made charts more brilliant. Horace left D natural and A natural to Fletcher but tried a few.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Were -- there was something I was gonna ask about that -- oh, in the arrangements -- when you're writing arrangements, did you consider a lot modulating from key to key, or did you tend to stay in one key? Now, I'm not thinking about having singers, but say, just a straight instrumental.

Instrumental? I find out -- I found out rather that if you would make little interludes after you're, say, first or second chorus and change keys -- have your out chorus in different keys -- the arrangement would sound more brilliant, and especially if you brought it up from say two or three steps up from the original one that you started out in. And a lot of times, you'd play with modulations going into that. It would lead you into that change of key, which would make the arrangement more interesting. I used to like this, plus the fact that it would give you a chance to play in more keys, and the musicians would like this because they wouldn't be limited, you know, to just plain E flat, or F--
Did you use -- sometimes did you
use strange keys like B or --
Or D natural, yeah, A natural.
We didn't do too much. I left that up to Fletcher, you know. This was his bag, but we would play in D flat a bit.

Yeah, five flats, and that's a hard thing. And then some of the tunes that were written in those days, even A flat was, you know, you had to keep your faculties about you. But everybody could play in C and F and B flat, you know, that was the crips (unintelligible), you know, but the guys go so that they wanted challenge some other keys. So I wrote a couple of things in D natural, A natural, and for a while, it sounded like scrambled eggs.
